title: Delhi Court Extends Detention of 'Cockroach' Leaders Ranka and Das by Two Days
excerpt: Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das, arrested after entering the newly banned Jantar Mantar protest site, will stay in custody while police question them further. Their party is demanding the election chief's resignation over the voter-list revision.
body:
• A Delhi court on Monday extended the judicial custody of Cockroach Janta Party leaders Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das by two more days, after Delhi Police sought more time to question them.
  • Ranka and Das were among 14 protesters who scaled barricades to enter Jantar Mantar last Tuesday, a day after the site was removed from the list of approved demonstration venues.
  • The youth-led movement is demanding Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar's resignation over a voter-list revision in which 130 million names were removed.
  • The party's legal head called the extension "an absolute mockery of the judicial system" and said it would challenge the order in a higher court.

An Indian court on Monday extended the detention of two leaders of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) by two more days, as a crackdown continues on near-daily protests against the government in New Delhi. Ashutosh Ranka and Saurav Das will remain in prison after Delhi Police requested extra time to question them, Al Jazeera and Reuters reported. Delhi Police did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Ranka and Das were among 14 protesters who climbed over barricades last week to enter the Jantar Mantar observatory, the historic protest venue in central Delhi, one day after it was removed from a list of approved demonstration sites. They unfurled the Indian flag and chanted slogans demanding the chief election commissioner's resignation before police detained them. A court later sent the activists to prison for five days; Monday's order adds two more.

"This is an absolute mockery of the judicial system."

— Ratna Singh, legal head, Cockroach Janta Party

The voter-list dispute behind the protests

The CJP, alongside opposition parties and left-wing student organisations, has led near-daily protests through October demanding the resignation of Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar. The protests target a revision of voter lists that critics say favours Prime Minister Narendra Modi's Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). In all, 130 million names were removed from the lists. The Election Commission says those names included 28 million people who have died, 63 million who have relocated and 30 million who could not be traced. It has denied favouring any party and says voters who were wrongly deleted can re-enrol.

The BJP has accused its rivals of trying to undermine democracy by wrongly questioning legitimate electoral processes. The latest demonstrations intensified after the Indian Express reported that Kumar's two deputies had raised concerns internally about voter list changes, registration procedures and digital systems, according to Reuters.

A movement that has grown beyond one protest

The detentions have widened the confrontation. CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke, student leaders and several supporters were also detained on Friday, as hundreds poured into central Delhi for a protest in support of Ranka and Das, Al Jazeera reported. Reuters describes the 'Cockroach' movement as one of the biggest political challenges to Modi and the BJP in his 12 years in power.

The party has won concessions before. A sit-in by the CJP and its supporters earlier this year forced the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan over exam paper leaks — a record that helps explain both the movement's confidence and the authorities' hard line at Jantar Mantar, where the legal status of protest itself is now part of the dispute: the venue was struck from the approved list the day before the 14 activists entered it.

What happens next

The CJP says it will challenge Monday's custody order in a higher court, and its supporters show no sign of ending the daily protests. The immediate questions are legal and political: whether a higher court cuts short Ranka and Das's detention, whether the Election Commission's defence of the voter-list revision holds as scrutiny of the deletions grows, and whether the Jantar Mantar ban becomes a wider fight over where protest is permitted in the capital. For now, the two leaders remain in custody, and the movement they lead remains on the street.
